alalal-e91896-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 3: whether falsehood can underlie faith, and whether necessary truth underlies it.

alalal-e91896-d1e115.summary: States the third question: whether falsehood could underlie faith.

alalal-e91896-d1e122.summary: First argument: faith was about the mediator, and Augustine says another way of healing our misery was possible, though none more fitting; if another had occurred, faith would have had a falsehood, so what is believed need not occur.

alalal-e91896-d1e143.summary: Second argument: Abraham believed he would sacrifice his son and did not, so he believed something false.

alalal-e91896-d1e154.summary: Third argument: falsehood can underlie the will, as Paul wanted to go to Spain and did not, so also faith.

alalal-e91896-d1e165.summary: Further: falsehood can underlie hope, since many hope for eternal life and will never have it, so also faith.

alalal-e91896-d1e178.summary: Fourth argument: if a priest at Mass elevates an unconsecrated host at the time of elevation, the bystanders believe it consecrated, which is false.

alalal-e91896-d1e196.summary: Sed contra: virtue is more certain than art (Aristotle), and no falsehood underlies art, so none underlies faith.

alalal-e91896-d1e207.summary: Second sed contra: faith on the way concerns what vision concerns in the homeland, and no falsehood can underlie vision.

alalal-e91896-d1e217.summary: Third sed contra: faith is assimilation to first truth, under which no falsehood can lie.

alalal-e91896-d1e226.summary: Fourth sed contra: divine truth surpasses the truth of all science; one adhering to known truth never falls into falsehood, since the false is not known, much less one adhering by faith.

alalal-e91896-d1e239.summary: Fifth sed contra: faith is argument and conviction of the truest unseen things, more certain to us than the divine nature presupposed in the articles; in secular sciences an argument's principle is never false, much less faith.

alalal-e91896-d1e259.summary: Asks further whether necessary or contingent truth underlies faith.

alalal-e91896-d1e268.summary: Introduces arguments that it is contingent.

alalal-e91896-d1e275.summary: First argument: as shown in Book I on omnipotence, contingency follows lower causes; the forgiveness of sins in the article depends on the will of the one forgiven, so it is not necessary.

alalal-e91896-d1e298.summary: Second argument: another way of liberation was possible, so this one was not necessary.

alalal-e91896-d1e314.summary: Sed contra: if the contingent underlay faith, since what can be can also not be, things could be otherwise than believed, and falsehood would underlie faith, which is impossible; so only necessary truth underlies faith.

alalal-e91896-d1e334.summary: Solution: only immutable truth underlies faith, but not necessary truth. As with predestination, there is a necessity of order: given the antecedent, the consequent immutably follows, and if it did not, the antecedent never was, though the consequent is contingent in itself. So if faith concerns something, it will immutably come about, though not necessary in itself; if it did not, faith never concerned it.
claims: Faith concerns immutably true, though not intrinsically necessary, truths.
The certainty of faith follows the necessity of order, like predestination.

alalal-e91896-d1e369.summary: Reply to the first: faith concerned the mediator, and given that, the mediator's coming immutably occurred; Augustine speaks of 'the mediator will be' considered in itself. Others answer ad hominem rather than by reason.

alalal-e91896-d1e387.summary: Examines an objection: Abraham believed the mediator would come, a true statement about the past and so necessary, making the contingent necessary. Some say the dictum depended on the future and escapes the necessity of the past; Albert rejects this, since the order is that of faith to the believed. Others distinguish believing that something is to come (the order of material causes, which may fail) from believing that it will be; this works for future contingents relative to lower causes, but faith and predestination involve the order of divine illumination, certain both in the order and in its outcome; and Abraham believed not just that Christ was to come but that he would be incarnate of his seed. So the first, common solution stands.

alalal-e91896-d1e472.summary: This also answers all similar objections.

alalal-e91896-d1e480.summary: Reply to Abraham's case: his belief that he would sacrifice his son was not an act of faith but an opinion arising from obedience, and falsehood can underlie that.
claims: Abraham's expectation to sacrifice Isaac was opinion, not faith.

alalal-e91896-d1e493.summary: Reply on will: will and hope do not have truth as proper object with falsehood as its opposite, as faith does; Paul's will, caused by human opinion, could be frustrated because the opinion was not fulfilled.

alalal-e91896-d1e513.summary: Likewise hope, the expectation of future beatitude, does not have truth as object; it can be frustrated of beatitude not by a defect of hope but of the one hoping, who does not persevere in good life until death, like Judas.
claims: Hope fails not through its own defect but through the hoper's failure to persevere.

alalal-e91896-d1e531.summary: Reply on the unconsecrated host: as answered earlier, a condition is supposed or added by the adorer, that the rite was duly celebrated, and then it is always true; anyway, believing this host is consecrated is an act of opinion, not of faith.
claims: Believing that a particular host is consecrated is opinion, not faith.

alalal-e91896.summary: Article 3 asks whether faith can have falsehood under it, and whether its truths are necessary or contingent. Cases such as other possible modes of redemption, Abraham's expected sacrifice of Isaac, frustrated wills and hopes, and an unconsecrated host suggest it can. The certainty of virtue and faith's assimilation to first truth suggest it cannot. Albert holds that no falsehood can underlie faith, which concerns immutably true but not intrinsically necessary truths. As with predestination, a necessity of order holds: what faith concerns will immutably come about, though contingent in itself, and if it did not, faith never concerned it. He rejects attempts to escape the objection by distinguishing 'will be' from 'is to come', since faith rests on certain divine illumination. Abraham's expectation and belief that a particular host is consecrated were opinion, not faith. Will and hope do not have truth as their object, and hope fails only through the hoper's failure to persevere.
claims: Faith concerns truths that are immutable by necessity of order, though contingent in themselves.
Particular human expectations, such as Abraham's or about a particular host, are opinion rather than faith.
